about: The Guarani the two new games added (their titles and the yes/no game's «No» button), checked against dictionaries, corpora and the app's own audited strings before release. Paths in 'sources' point to the reviewer's local copies of the public corpora it searched.

verdicts.note:
The Guarani is correct and natural. It is e- (imperative to one child) + hendu «oír, escuchar» + porã «bien». It is built exactly like the audited «Ehecha porã» (g313, g325), and it is the ordinary way to tell one child «escuchá bien» (to the whole class: «Pehendu porã»). Tatoeba gives the same verb + porã for «Listen very closely» («Ehenduporãitéke»).

No suffix is wanted in a title:
- -ke («Ehendúke», «Ehendu porãke») makes it an insistent order.
- -mi or -mína turns it into «please listen» and drops «bien».
- The app's other instruction titles and buttons are plain imperatives («Ehecha ha ehendu», «Ehendu ha eiporavo», «Emopu'ã ñe'ẽ», «Ehendu»).

Write porã as a separate word, as in «Ehecha porã».

One fix outside the Guarani: the Spanish shown under a title is read as its translation. YesNo.dc.html:28–29 prints it directly under the Guarani, and «¿Sí o no?» is not what «Ehendu porã» says. The audit rejected exactly this kind of mismatch:
- g260: «Mombe'u» under «Cuento del cielo»;
- g313 and g325: «Ehecha porã» must be glossed «Mirá bien».

So gloss it «Escuchá bien», or «Escuchá bien: ¿sí o no?» to keep the question. That puts the translation first, as in g325. Change it in GAMES.yesno.es, which also feeds Tonight's row.

Confidence: high for the Guarani. None of the MEC texts I could search uses the phrase, so the verdict rests on dictionaries, corpora and the app's own audited pattern.

verdicts.note:
Right word and right school spelling.

It is the plain answer «no». Guasch gives «no: ahániri, nahániri (simple no)», and Estigarribia's grammar pairs (n)ahániri 'no' with heẽ 'yes'.

Accent: na-HÁ-ni-ri is stressed on há. A Guarani word without an accent mark is read with stress on its last syllable, so the acute is required. «nahaniri» would put the stress on -ri and is a misspelling: 1 hit against 38 in Jojajovai, and the same 1 against 38 in Guarani Wikipedia. The MEC itself writes «nahániriramo» (Programa de estudio, 2.º grado).

«Ahániri» is a correct variant (Guasch, Galeano Olivera, Tatoeba «Ahániri.»), but much rarer, so keep Nahániri.

«Ani» would be wrong. It forbids and goes before a verb («Ani ndepochy» = «No te enojes»), so as an answer to «¿es un perro?» it would read as «¡no lo hagas!».

It pairs naturally with «Héẽ»:
- Galeano Olivera lists Héẽ as the adverb of affirmation, and nahániri first among those of negation.
- Tatoeba has «Yes.» = «Héẽ.» and «No.» = «Nahániri.».
- A Jojajovai line sets the two against each other: «ombohovái héê, ha nahániri» = «la respuesta es un sí, y no un no».

The spelling of Héẽ itself is still open (Estigarribia writes heẽ; Tatoeba also has Hẽe), but that does not affect Nahániri. As a button label: capital N and no punctuation, like «Héẽ».

Confidence: high.

verdicts.note:
Keep it.

japyhy is the dictionary verb for «agarrar, atrapar», not only for «tomá»:
- Guasch lists it under atrapar, asir and capturar/prender.
- The Argentine Avañe'ẽ dictionary glosses it «agarrar, tomar, abarcar, atrapar».
- The catching sense is attested for people and things that get away: Guarani Wikipedia «ojejapyhy haguã Nicolás Maduro-pe», «Hesu Kirito ojejapyhy».
- A Guarani software glossary renders «Capturar» as «Ejapyhy».

«Tomá» is the same verb said while handing something over, just as Paraguayan Spanish «agarrá» means both «tomá» and «atrapá». The floating stars and «Atrapá la estrella» under the title make the catching reading clear.

No other word is needed:
- Guarani has no article.
- A non-human object such as mbyja takes no -pe. The app's «Emopu'ã ñe'ẽ» = «Armá la palabra» has the same shape.
- «pe mbyja» would mean «esa estrella», and Jopara «la mbyja» is not school style.

The other verbs are worse for a children's app:
- «Eipyhy» (pyhy) also means atrapar, and Guarani Wikipedia uses it for catching fish and insects. But Guasch notes that pyhy is often used in an obscene sense («coger»).
- «Ehupyty» means «alcanzar, conseguir», and the app already says «Rehupyty peteĩ mbyja.» for «Ganaste una estrella». It would blur catching a star with earning one.
- «Ejagarra» is a Spanish loan.

Confidence: medium, for two reasons. No corpus sentence I found has japyhy with a thrown or flying object. And one unverified Scribd dictionary also gives japyhy a vulgar sense; that sense needs a person as the object and cannot arise with mbyja. A teacher's glance would settle both points.
